name: Ts’ui Hao
bio: Ts’ui Hao is dated by Giles to the 8th century AD. His poem here is set at the Yellow Crane Tower, a subject long associated with his name.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poems.title: Home Longings
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.text:
Here a mortal once sailed up to heaven on a crane,
And the Yellow-Crane Kiosque will for ever remain; "
But the bird flew away and will come back no more,
Though the white clouds are there as the white clouds of yore.

Away to the east lie fair forests of trees.
From the flowers on the west comes a scent-laden breeze,
Yet my eyes daily turn to their far-away home.
Beyond the broad River, its waves, and its foam.

poems.title: Boating Song of the Yo Eh
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.text:
O light we glide through forest green,
By misty shore and gaunt ravine.
    And whether we tarry or drift along
    The clouds and the birds around us throng,
And mirrored mountains' nodding brows
Follow the wake of our flying prows.

Now song returns from rock to rock;
Now soundless glades our silence mock.
    Sunbeam and shadow elves at play
    Beckon our wandering wills to stray.
Ah furl your sails! ah furl your sails!
The last wind down the valley fails.

poems.title: A Song of Ch'ang-kan
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
I

"Tell me, where do you live? —
Near here, by the fishing-pool?
Let's hold our boats together, let's see
If we belong in the same town."

II

"Yes, I live here, by the river;
I have sailed on it many and many a time.
Both of us born in Ch'ang-kan, you and I!
Why haven't we always known each other? "

poems.title: The Yellow Crane Terrace
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Where long ago a yellow crane bore a sage to heaven,
Nothing is left now but the Yellow Crane Terrace.
The yellow crane never revisited earth,
And white clouds are flying without him for ever.
. . . Every tree in Han-yang becomes clear in the water,
And Parrot Island is a nest of^sweet grasses;
But I look toward home, and twilight grows dark
With a mist of grief on the river waves.

poems.title: Passing Through Hua-yin
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Lords of the capital, sharp, unearthly,
The Great Flower's three points pierce through heaven.
Clouds are parting above the Temple of the Warring Emperor,
Rain dries on the mountain, on the Giant's Palm.
Ranges and rivers are the strength of this western gate,
Whence roads and trails lead downward into China.
. . . O pilgrim of fame, O seeker of profit,
Why not remain here and lengthen your days?

poems.title: 黃鶴樓 (Huang he lou)
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.note: 七言律詩. Also titled 登黃鶴樓.
poems.text:
昔人已乘黃鶴去，此地空餘黃鶴樓。
黃鶴一去不復返，白雲千載空悠悠。
晴川歷歷漢陽樹，芳草萋萋鸚鵡洲。
日暮鄉關何處是？煙波江上使人愁。

poems.title: 行經華陰 (Xing jing hua yin)
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
岧嶢太華俯鹹京，天外三峯削不成。
武帝祠前雲欲散，仙人掌上雨初晴。
河山北枕秦關險，驛樹西連漢畤平。
借問路傍名利客，無如此處學長生。

poems.title: 長幹行·君家何處住 (Chang gan xing, jun jia he chu zhu)
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
君家何處住，妾住在橫塘。
停船暫借問，或恐是同鄉。

poems.title: 長幹行·家臨九江水 (Chang gan xing, jia lin jiu jiang shui)
poems.author: Ts’ui Hao
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
家臨九江水，來去九江側。
同是長幹人，生小不相識。
